extracted.intended_audience: Cochrane review authors, systematic review teams, and information specialists/librarians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing comprehensive search strategies and sources for Cochrane systematic reviews of interventions, including locating unpublished trials, using trial registers, regulatory sources, grey literature, and structuring database searches. Emphasises roles for information specialists and methods to maximise sensitivity while maintaining reasonable precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching by contacting relevant individuals and organizations (C31)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact relevant individuals and organisations for information about unpublished or ongoing studies. (Labelled 'Highly desirable')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send comprehensive lists of relevant articles and study records plus eligibility criteria to first authors of included-study reports; ask if they know of additional studies (ongoing, completed, terminated; published or unpublished). Send similar requests to other experts, pharmaceutical companies and interested organisations. Set up project websites listing identified studies and invite submissions of unlisted studies. Email contact tends to be more successful than other methods. Methods used successfully include combined email and digital/social platforms (ResearchGate, LinkedIn). Contacting trial authors, clinical trial units, trial methodologists, and manufacturers can identify otherwise-unretrieved data and sometimes change review conclusions. Consider RIAT methodology and Freedom of Information Act requests where appropriate. Document any successful contacts and the impact on review results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching trials registers (C27) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search trials registers and repositories of results, where relevant to the topic, through ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO ICTRP portal and other appropriate sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searches should be as extensive as possible to reduce publication bias. Do not rely on ICTRP alone — search ClinicalTrials.gov separately because not all ClinicalTrials.gov records may be retrievable via the ICTRP portal. Do not limit searches of trials registers or portals by trial status (e.g. 'completed' vs 'ongoing') or by trial phase because these fields may be inaccurate or not up to date. Include trial-results postings (where available) as these can provide results for completed/terminated trials not published elsewhere. Consult the Technical Supplement for searching guidance and key registers to include. Consider other national or specialty registers and portals as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching regulatory agency sources and clinical study reports (CSRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search regulatory agency sources for trial information including clinical study reports, which provide detailed methods and results submitted for marketing-authorisation applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisations (e.g., AHRQ, IQWiG, Institute of Medicine, Cochrane) recommend searching regulatory sources (EMA, FDA, TGA, PMDA, Health Canada, etc.) for CSRs and related documents. Regulatory sites may also host trial-register-like records (e.g., EUCTR, EU Clinical Trials Information Service, Drugs@FDA, EUDAMED). CSRs often provide more complete information on methods and outcomes than journal articles or register records. Review teams may need additional guidance and support to identify and use regulatory data; consult the Technical Supplement and Chapter 5 (Section 5.5.6) for details on locating and extracting CSR data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching for grey literature (C28) (Highly desirable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search relevant grey literature sources such as reports, dissertations, theses and conference abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reports published outside traditional commercial publishing. Consider searching the internet, handsearching journals, and searching full texts electronically where available. Do not apply document-format exclusions (e.g., excluding letters) routinely because they may contain important trial information or warnings. Consult the Technical Supplement for sources and methods. Aim for extensive searches to reduce publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching within previous reviews (C29) (Highly desirable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search within previous reviews on the same topic to identify potentially relevant studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine earlier systematic reviews and their included/excluded studies as part of comprehensive searching. Use previous reviews to identify older or hard-to-find trials and to inform search terms and strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking reference lists (C30) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check reference lists in included studies and any relevant systematic reviews identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference-list checking is mandatory as part of an extensive search to reduce the risk of missing eligible studies. Use reference lists to find additional trials and relevant reports not captured by database or register searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing search strategies: plan factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Search strategy design should consider the nature/type of interventions, complexity of the review question (including conceptual frameworks), time periods specified in the protocol, geographic considerations, eligible study designs, validated methodological filters, whether unpublished data are sought, and specific eligibility criteria for adverse effects, economic, or qualitative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve a medical/healthcare librarian or information specialist for robust searches. Use PICO elements and study-design considerations to select subject headings and text words. Tailor searches for specific needs (e.g., adverse effects, economic evidence, qualitative studies) and document decisions in the protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring search strategies for bibliographic databases (C32) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform the structure of search strategies around the main concepts of the review, using appropriate elements from PICO and study design; maximize sensitivity whilst striving for reasonable precision. Ensure correct use of 'AND' and 'OR' operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general databases (e.g., MEDLINE) a typical search will have three sets of terms: (i) population/health condition; (ii) intervention(s); (iii) study design (often a randomized-trials filter). Within-concept terms are combined with OR, concepts combined with AND. Avoid the NOT operator where possible. Recognise exceptions where PICO/Baseline structure is unsuitable (diagnostic test accuracy, prognosis, qualitative, complex interventions) and adopt tailored approaches in those cases (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailored approaches for complex or non-PICO questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When PICO-based structuring is unsuitable (e.g., complex interventions, diagnostic accuracy, prognosis, realist or qualitative reviews), use alternative or multiple search approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: non-PICO question breakdowns; single-concept searches (e.g., intervention alone); breaking compound concepts into subconcepts; multi-stranded/multi-faceted series of searches; iterative searches; citation searching; machine-learning assisted prioritisation/categorisation; visual search-building aids (2DSearch, searchrefiner, Nested Knowledge); and using AI chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude) for suggestions. Consult the Technical Supplement and evidence cited for these methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensitivity versus precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Searches should seek to maximise sensitivity (recall) while striving for reasonable precision; recognise trade-offs between identifying as many relevant reports as possible and retrieving many non-relevant records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity = relevant reports retrieved / total relevant reports. Precision = relevant reports retrieved / total reports retrieved. High-sensitivity searches will lower precision and increase screening workload, but abstract screening is usually rapid (estimated 60–120 abstracts/hour). Design searches with the anticipated screening capacity in mind; consider alternative strategies if volume is unmanageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms (C33) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop search strategies using an appropriate combination of controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH, Emtree, with 'exploded' terms) and free-text terms (spelling variants, synonyms, acronyms, truncation, proximity operators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize strategies for each database because controlled vocabularies and indexing differ. Ensure MeSH/Emtree terms are exploded where appropriate. Use a wide range of free-text terms, truncation and wildcards as needed. Developing a search is iterative — modify terms based on retrieved records. See Technical Supplement for methods (text-mining, filters, examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, date and document-format restrictions — caution and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid restricting searches by language or document format to reduce bias; justify any date or format restrictions used in the search strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict searches by language; if language restrictions are applied, justify them and consider recording excluded-language reports as 'studies awaiting classification' if data cannot be extracted. Date limits may be used if justified (e.g., device approval date) but arbitrary date limits are not recommended. Be cautious about which date field is used (create date, entry date, update date, publication date) and consider searching wider date ranges to account for inconsistent dates. Do not routinely exclude letters or comments; consider preprints as potentially relevant, especially for emerging topics. If translation or data extraction help is needed for non-English reports, seek assistance (e.g., Cochrane Engage). Document and report any restrictions.
